# Project-Approved Words and Rules

> [[ASD-STE100_ISSUE9.pdf]]  `2026-10-12`  `d1f4ea9e7cd6`

The words and the writing rules this project approves beyond ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, Issue 9.
The asd-ste skill writes with the words as it writes with the approved words of [ste-dictionary.json](ste-dictionary.json), and by the rules as it writes by the House Rules of [ste-rules.md](ste-rules.md).
`check_ste.py --custom` reads the table of words, and `check_ste.py` checks each rule that the table of rules marks as checked.
Each STE file declares this file in its header quote, `> [[ste-custom]]`, as House Rule 5 of [ste-rules.md](ste-rules.md) tells, and `depends_on.py record` records its fingerprint.
A change to this file makes `depends_on.py check` report each STE file CHANGED, but they need not be checked again after each change.
After the last change of the day, run [draft.py](../scripts/draft.py) `recheck` once, from the workspace root, with a `--root` for each workspace folder, and commit what it records on its own.
It checks a draft again as `run step 3` does and a file that a draft replaced with `check_ste.py --ste`, records this file in each one that passes, and lists each one that fails with its `[FAIL]` lines, for you to correct.
The draft you are working on is the exception: run step 3 on it at once; Steps 6 and 7 run it themselves when this file changed after its last check.

## Words

- Each word is approved in the parts of speech and the forms that its row gives, and in its meaning only.
- `check_ste.py` accepts each one as an approved word, and an `[INFO]` line names each one that a file uses, so that a reviewer sees every word that Issue 9 does not approve.
- A word joins the table only on the user's decision, and its Why cell says when and why.
- `check_ste.py` finds the table by its header row: keep its five cells as they are.
  Write the parts of speech as the dictionary writes them - `n`, `v`, `adj`, `adv`, `prep`, `conj`, `pron` - separated by commas.
  Write the forms separated by commas, or `—` when the word has none.

## Rules

- Each rule is a writing rule that the user adds for this project, beyond the rules of Issue 9 and the House Rules of ste-rules.md; a draft follows each one.
- A rule joins the table only on the user's decision, and its Why cell says when and why.
- The Checked cell says how the rule is checked: `check_ste.py` gives a `[WARN]` line where the prose may break it, and a person reads each one and decides; `—` means that only the reviewer checks it.

| Rule | Example | Checked | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Do not use two negatives to give a positive meaning: write the positive statement. | "Do not write a command incorrectly." becomes "Write each command correctly." | `check_ste.py` gives a `[WARN]` line, "double negative?", for a negative word followed in the same clause by a word that a negative prefix makes from an approved word | 2026-10-17, the user, while tw-keep-english.md was reviewed (Task 32, step 2.3): Issue 9 has no rule about double negatives, and two negatives make the reader stop to find the positive meaning. |
| Keep the name that the source gives an item, such as a rule, as it is, between quotation marks. | "The scripted-versus-not rule of skill-writing.md" becomes "the "scripted-versus-not" rule of skill-writing.md", not "the rule of skill-writing.md about scripts". | — | 2026-10-18, the user, while README-tmp.md was reviewed (Task 32.10): the draft had written "the rule of skill-writing.md about scripts" for the scripted-versus-not rule, but check-skill, gen-skill and three READMEs give the rule that name, and STE gives one item one name (rule 1.11); skill-writing-ste.md had kept "no forward-reference" between quotation marks for the same reason. |
